cards.title: Ohm's law
cards.simple: Voltage = Current × Resistance (V = I × R). More resistance means less current for the same voltage. A loose or corroded joint adds resistance, so the load gets less voltage.

cards.title: Electrical power
cards.simple: Power = Voltage × Current (P = V × I = I² × R). A 24V 5W lamp draws about 0.21 A. Power lost in a bad joint turns into heat, which is why burnt terminals are a clue.

cards.title: A circuit must be a complete loop
cards.simple: Current only flows if there is an unbroken path from supply, through the load, and back to 0V. Any open point (blown fuse, open contact, broken wire, loose terminal, missing ground) stops the whole circuit. Fault finding means finding that open point.

cards.title: How a relay works
cards.simple: A relay is a switch worked by a magnet. When its coil (terminals A1-A2) gets voltage, it pulls in and changes its contacts: normally open (NO, e.g. 13-14) close, normally closed (NC, e.g. 11-12) open. No coil voltage = contacts stay at rest. Check the coil side and the contact side separately.

cards.title: Fuses and breakers
cards.simple: A fuse or breaker opens the circuit when current is too high, to protect the wiring. A blown fuse is a symptom, not the cause: before replacing, look for a short circuit or overloaded load. Check with power off: a good fuse reads near 0 Ω.

cards.title: Voltage drop in cables and joints
cards.simple: Every cable and joint has some resistance, so voltage drops along the way: Vdrop = 2 × length × current × 0.0175 ÷ cross-section (copper, mm²). Under load, a healthy circuit should lose only a little. A big drop across one joint or contact means that point is bad.

cards.title: 4-20 mA current loop
cards.simple: Analog sensors often send their value as a current: 4 mA = minimum, 20 mA = maximum. Because zero is 4 mA, 0 mA means a broken wire or dead sensor, so the controller can spot it. Below about 3.8 mA or above 20.5 mA is normally flagged as a fault. Measure the current in series, or the voltage across the input resistor.

cards.title: Freewheel diode on coils
cards.simple: When a coil is switched off, its magnetic field collapses and makes a high voltage spike. A diode (or RC/varistor) across the coil absorbs it to protect the PLC output or switch. A shorted diode blows the fuse or the output; a missing one can kill outputs over time. Fitted backwards, it is a dead short.

cards.title: Voltage test method (live)
cards.simple: With the circuit switched ON, put the black probe on 0V and move the red probe along the path from supply to load. Where the voltage disappears, the open point is just before that spot. Measuring across a closed contact should read about 0V; reading full voltage across it means it is open. Splitting the path in half each time finds the fault fastest.

cards.title: Ground / return path faults
cards.simple: The return to 0V is half the circuit and is often forgotten. A load can have full voltage at its input and still not work if its ground is open. Test: measure voltage across the load itself; supply present at the input but not across the load means the return side is open.

cards.title: PLC digital outputs
cards.simple: A digital output switches a load on and off. A sourcing (PNP) output gives +24V to the load; a sinking (NPN) output connects the load to 0V. An output LED that is ON only means the PLC wants it on: always measure the actual voltage at the terminal. Outputs have a current limit; overload can trip or damage them.

cards.title: PLC digital inputs
cards.simple: A digital input reads ON when its voltage is above a threshold (often about 11-15V on a 24V system) and OFF below a lower threshold. A voltage in between, from a bad contact or long cable, gives unreliable readings. Check the input LED and measure the voltage at the input terminal.

cards.title: Common engine sensors
cards.simple: PT100 temperature sensors are resistors: 100 Ω at 0 °C, about 138.5 Ω at 100 °C; open = very high reading, short = very low. Thermocouples make a small mV signal that rises with temperature. Pressure transmitters usually give 4-20 mA or 0-10 V. Speed pickups (inductive) make an AC signal that rises with rpm.

cards.title: CAN bus basics
cards.simple: CAN is a two-wire data bus (CAN-H and CAN-L) linking controllers. Each end has a 120 Ω terminating resistor, so with power OFF you should measure about 60 Ω between CAN-H and CAN-L. About 120 Ω = one terminator missing; near 0 Ω = short; open = broken bus. With power on, CAN-H is about 2.5-3.5V and CAN-L about 1.5-2.5V.

cards.title: Terminal and connector faults
cards.simple: On engines, vibration, heat and moisture make terminals loose or corroded. They may pass a meter test with no load but fail under current. Look for discoloration, green corrosion and pushed-back pins. Wiggle-test the wiring while watching the reading.

cards.title: Open circuit vs short circuit
cards.simple: Open circuit: the path is broken, no current flows, the load is dead, and fuses stay intact. Short circuit: current bypasses the load straight to 0V, current is very high, and the fuse blows or the output trips. Short to ground and short to supply can also make a part look always ON or always OFF.

cards.title: Diodes and LEDs
cards.simple: A diode lets current flow one way only (anode to cathode), dropping about 0.7V for silicon. An LED drops about 2-3V and needs a series resistor. Fitted backwards, an LED stays dark. Meter diode test: one direction reads about 0.5-0.7V, the other reads open.

cards.title: Series and parallel
cards.simple: Series: the same current flows through everything; resistances add (R = R1 + R2); one open breaks all. Parallel: the same voltage is across each branch; total resistance is lower (1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2); one branch can fail while the others keep working.

cards.title: 24V DC control systems
cards.simple: Most engine and panel controls run on 24V DC. Many devices accept roughly 18-32V, but check the manual for each one. With the engine running, the charging voltage is often around 27-28V. Low battery voltage during cranking can reset controllers.

cards.title: Insulation resistance test
cards.simple: An insulation tester (megger) applies a high test voltage between a conductor and earth to find leaking insulation. Healthy wiring reads in the megohms. Always disconnect electronics (controllers, sensors, PLC cards) before testing, or the test voltage can destroy them.
